This captivating rug takes its inspiration from an unusual 17th century ?Dragon Carpet? made in the Azerbaijan region of the Islamic empire. Originally in the James F. Ballard Collection and now in a museum, it reflects carpet-weaving traditions of villages throughout the Caucasus. While rugs from royal workshops typically had flowing floral patterns, provincial weavings were more strongly geometric as seen here in the motif of highly stylized dragons. The original is boldly colored in reds, blues and tan. The modern version is reimagined in sparkling tones of seaglass with highlights in sunlight and flame, creating an almost translucent vision of luminescent color.

Not surprisingly, the original of this rug, a 17th century masterpiece, once graced an Imperial Collection (Rijks Museum, Amsterdam). The motif, a Persian ?Vase-Carpet?, is extremely rich and detailed with abundant floral life. Like all carpets of this class, it is characterized by vivid colorization. Its absolutely spectacular polychrome pattern features 12 colors with ground pigments predominating green, orange and brown; its design utilizes those colors plus wine-red, rose, blues, greens, yellow and white. The border is enhanced by sinuous arabesques. The modern Nourison interpretation captures its essential beauty with an exuberance of design in the classic Vase pattern. A glittering green-gold predominates the color story, with equally rich effect in details of bronze, lapis and magenta. A narrow border frames this fine piece with artful delicacy.

An enchanted forest grows in the secret glade enclosed within the borders of this spectacular rug, inspired by a treasure currently on loan to New York?s Metropolitan Museum of Art. This captivating rug takes its inspiration from an unusual 17th century ?Dragon Carpet? made in the Azerbaijan region of the Islamic empire. Originally in the James F. Ballard Collection and now in a museum, it reflects carpet-weaving traditions of villages throughout the Caucasus. While rugs from royal workshops typically had flowing floral patterns, provincial weavings were more strongly geometric as seen here in the motif of highly stylized dragons. The original is boldly colored in reds, blues and tan. The modern version is reimagined in sparkling tones of seaglass with highlights in sunlight and flame, creating an almost translucent vision of luminescent color.

Not surprisingly, the original of this rug, a 17th century masterpiece, once graced an Imperial Collection (Rijks Museum, Amsterdam). A glittering green-gold predominates the color story, with equally rich effect in details of bronze, lapis and magenta. A narrow border frames this fine piece with artful delicacy.

?No more exquisite harmony was ever realized in any Persian Rug.? Thus was the original silk Isfahan rug of Central Persia described when placed at auction by the Doris Duke Collection ? once the property of that fabled heiress. Through scrolling floral vinery and arabesques, the golden-grounded original commands attention with regal poise. Nourison reinterprets this magnificent piece, capturing its glory with exceptional intricacy in the vining pattern and rich, coppery tones with delicate blue and green detailing on a lusciously patinated ground. As commanding of admiration as its original, this highly refined design displays all the qualities of Nourison?s renowned artistry and meticulous craftsmanship.

Order is attained through a symmetrical pattern radiating out from a line of central palmettes and enclosed within a broad tripartite border. Strikingly brilliant, with a flowing yet symmetrical aesthetic, the marvelous vitality of this masterwork fills the room with energy and warmth.
